revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Captain Vega’s Treasure Square
revealWordProblem.text: Captain Vega buried treasure at the four corners of a square. Three corners are at (2, 2), (2, 6), and (6, 6). She always plots her corners in Quadrant I. What ordered pair is the fourth corner, and what is the side length of the square?
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: The fourth corner is (6, 2). The square has a side length of 4 units, because from (2, 2) to (6, 2) is 6 − 2 = 4 units and from (2, 2) to (2, 6) is 6 − 2 = 4 units.

conceptIntro.heading: Push further — How do you plot a point on the coordinate plane?
conceptIntro.intro: You already can do this. In this group we go deeper: trickier numbers, a second way to see it, and explaining why it works — not just getting the answer.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Always start at the origin (0, 0), move right/left first, then up/down — and you can explain why it works, even when it gets tricky.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I will plot the point (5, 4). The 5 is the x-coordinate, and the 4 is the y-coordinate.
I start at the origin, which is (0, 0).
First I move 5 units to the right along the x-axis.
Then I move 4 units up. I place my dot. That is the point (5, 4).

onLevel.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Move right
workedExample.work: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis. Good.

workedExample.label: Move up
workedExample.work: Move 4 units up, because the pair has a 4 in it.

onLevel.correctWork: The y-coordinate is 0, not 4. After moving 4 right, the up move is 0 units, so the point stays on the x-axis at (4, 0). The student reused the x-value instead of reading the second number (0).
hints: What is the SECOND number in (4, 0), and how far up does it tell you to move?
A y-coordinate of 0 means do not move up at all — the point sits right on the x-axis at (4, 0).

onLevel.title: Extending — Miscounted Grid Lines

workedExample.label: Move along the x-axis
workedExample.work: Start at the origin (0, 0) and count 7 units to the right.

workedExample.label: Move along the y-axis
workedExample.work: Count up from the x-axis: 1, 2, 3, 4 — stop on 4.

onLevel.correctWork: The x-axis itself is 0, not 1. Counting up correctly: 1, 2, 3 — the third count lands on y = 3, so the point is (7, 3), not (7, 4). The student started counting one gridline too high by treating the x-axis as unit 1 instead of unit 0.
hints: When you count up from the x-axis, is the x-axis itself unit 0 or unit 1?
The x-axis is 0. The first line above it is 1, the second is 2, the third is 3. So 3 units up lands on y = 3, not y = 4.

onLevel.prompt: A student says that (3, 5) and (5, 3) are the same point because they use the same numbers. Is the student correct? Explain why or why not, and describe where each point is located on the coordinate plane.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: The student is ___ because (3, 5) means ___ while (5, 3) means ___. The ORDER matters because ___.
onLevel.hint: Compare what each coordinate pair tells you about horizontal and vertical moves.
hints: Both pairs use 3 and 5, but look at which number sits in the x (first) spot in each pair.
Describe each point's moves separately: (3, 5) = right ?, up ?; (5, 3) = right ?, up ?. Compare the two paths.
First step: for (3, 5), go right 3 and up 5. Now do (5, 3)'s moves and check whether you land on the same dot.

onLevel.stem: Spot 1 — Captain Vega's first clue says the Sandy Dock is right 7 and up 2 from the origin. Which ordered pair names the Sandy Dock?
onLevel.explanation: The x-coordinate is the sideways move (right 7) and the y-coordinate is the up move (up 2), so the Sandy Dock is (7, 2).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.

extending.stem: Spot 2 — The map marks the Lookout Tower at (4, 9). What does the 4 tell you to do from the origin?
choices: Move 4 units to the right along the x-axis
Move 4 units up along the y-axis
extending.explanation: The first number in (x, y) is the x-coordinate, so 4 means move 4 units to the right along the x-axis before moving up.
choiceFeedback: The first number controls horizontal movement—check which number moves you up.
With a positive first number, you move right—not left.

extending.stem: Spot 3 — Vega writes: 'The Coconut Grove is 3 across and 8 up.' Which point on the map is the Coconut Grove?
extending.explanation: Across (3) is the x-coordinate and up (8) is the y-coordinate, so the Coconut Grove is at (3, 8).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.

extending.title: Level 2 Extension — Captain Vega's Misread Coordinate

workedExample.label: Read the x-coordinate
workedExample.work: Move 3 units to the right along the x-axis.

workedExample.label: Read the y-coordinate
workedExample.work: Move 1 unit up along the y-axis.

workedExample.label: Plot the point
workedExample.work: Place the flag where (3, 1) would go.

extending.correctWork: The x move is correct (3 right), but the y-coordinate is 6, not 1. The navigator should move 6 units up, placing the flag at (3, 6) — not (3, 1).
hints: Look at the SECOND number in (3, 6). How many units up should the flag move?
y = 6, so move 6 units up after the 3 right. The point is (3, 6), not (3, 1).

extending.stem: Which ordered pair names a point 3 units right and 7 units up from the origin?
extending.explanation: The first coordinate is horizontal (right 3), the second is vertical (up 7). So (3, 7).
choiceFeedback: You swapped the x and y—the first number is horizontal, second is vertical.
Remember the x-coordinate tells you how far horizontally.
The first number is the horizontal (right/left) distance.
hints: Re-read the moves: 3 units right, then 7 units up. Which move comes first in an ordered pair?
An ordered pair is (x, y): x is the right/left distance, y is the up/down distance. Match each move to its slot.
Start at the origin and go right 3 — that 3 is the x, the first number. Now decide where the 'up 7' goes.

extending.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?
extending.explanation: The origin is where the x-axis and y-axis cross, at (0, 0).
choiceFeedback: The origin is where both axes cross, where both values are zero.
Both coordinates at the origin are 0 — not mixed with 1.
Check both the x and y values at the origin.
hints: The origin is the exact spot where the x-axis and y-axis cross. Picture that crossing point.
Ask: how far right have you moved at the origin? How far up? Those two distances are the coordinates.
At the crossing point you haven't moved right at all, so x = 0. Now figure out the y-value the same way.

extending.stem: A point is at (6, 2). What does the 6 tell you?
extending.explanation: The first number (x-coordinate) tells you horizontal movement. 6 means go right 6 units from the origin.
choiceFeedback: The first number controls horizontal movement—check which number moves you up.
With a positive first number, you move right—not left.
Double-check: verify the math step-by-step against the question.
hints: In (6, 2), the 6 is the FIRST number. First and second positions have different jobs.
First number = x = horizontal (right/left). Second number = y = vertical (up/down). Positive means right or up.
The 6 sits in the x spot and it's positive, so it describes a horizontal move. Which direction is positive x?

extending.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Move up
workedExample.work: Move 5 units UP along the y-axis.

workedExample.label: Move right
workedExample.work: Move 2 units to the right. Place the dot at (2, 5).

extending.correctWork: The student moved UP first. The FIRST number (5) is the x-coordinate, so move 5 units RIGHT; then the SECOND number (2) is the y-coordinate, so move 2 units UP. The point is (5, 2), not (2, 5).
hints: Which direction does the first number in (x, y) tell you to move — right or up?
The first number is always the horizontal (right) move. Here that is 5 right, then 2 up.

extending.label: Plot these points to reveal a hidden shape: (1, 1), (1, 5), (6, 5), (6, 1)
extending.hint: Start at the origin (0, 0) for each point. Move right first, then up.
hints: Each pair is (x, y). For point A(1, 1) both moves are just 1 unit.
For every point: start at (0, 0), slide right x units along the bottom, then climb up y units.
Plot A first: right 1, up 1. Then B(1, 5): same x, so it sits straight above A — count up to 5.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Graph on the Coordinate Plane is swapping the order of the coordinates — moving up/down first instead of right/left first. For example, when plotting (5, 2), students often move up 5 and right 2, landing on the wrong point (2, 5) instead of (5, 2). Remember: the x-coordinate (first number) always tells you how far to move right or left along the x-axis; the y-coordinate (second number) tells you how far up or down along the y-axis.

diagram.caption: Each ordered pair (x, y) places a stop: read x for the sideways move, y for the up move — connect Base to Pickup to Delivery and back to see the triangle.

connect.scenario: A drone delivery company programs flight paths using coordinate pairs. A drone starts at the warehouse (0, 0), flies to pickup at (3, 6), then delivers to (8, 2), then returns to base (0, 0).
connect.promptQuestion: How do ordered pairs help the drone navigate? What shape does the flight path make?
connect.prompt: The drone uses ordered pairs because the first number controls ___ movement and the second controls ___. The path makes a ___ shape.

exitTicket.stem: Explain your thinking — Point P is located 6 units right and 3 units up from the origin. What ordered pair names point P?
exitTicket.explanation: Right 6 = x-coordinate of 6, Up 3 = y-coordinate of 3. The ordered pair is (6, 3).
choiceFeedback: You swapped them — the x-coordinate (right) comes first.
The point moved up 3 too — the y-coordinate isn't zero.
It moved right 6 first — the x-coordinate isn't zero.
hints: Point P's moves: 6 right, then 3 up. In an ordered pair the horizontal move is written first.
Build the pair as (x, y) = (right distance, up distance). Match each number to its move before choosing.
Right 6 means the x-coordinate is 6, so the pair starts with 6. Now place the 'up 3' move in its slot.
